question: How is the chosen tool stored and brought onto the centre axis?

tools: Magnet poker with hook / pry tip
Spare bit held straight in a magnetic cartridge (1/4 in insert bit + 6x3 mm magnet)

shared_checks.push load path: work push goes into spring pawls behind the cartridge's rear collar in the barrel (not into the feed)
shared_checks.pull load path: pull on the tool goes into the barrel's front lip (bore 12.6 < cartridge 15.0)

options.name: Revolver cylinder (offset), straight push
options.principle: Five chambers in a cylinder whose axis sits 14.5 mm off the tool axis. Turning it brings one chamber onto the centre line behind the barrel; a belt carriage pushes that cartridge straight forward into the barrel and later pulls it back into the same chamber.
motors: ST3215-HS spin (1:1 gear to the barrel)
STS3032 feed (2:1 to a GT2 belt)
options.risk: Body is lopsided: it reaches 41 mm on the cylinder side and 22 mm on the other.
pros: Straight push: no bend for a long tool to jam in
Any tool to any tool in the same time, never passes another
No electronics on a turning part: no slip ring
Closest to a real revolver: proven mechanism
cons: No angling cam: the cylinder turns the tool onto the centre line instead
Lopsided body (centre of mass 7 mm off axis)

options.name: Keep the selector cam (as built)
options.principle: Four fingers on a spinning wrist; one drum cam swings one finger up onto the axis, the rest fold back outside.
options.risk: Waits up to 6.2 s; tools ride outside; servo bus through a slip ring untested.
pros: Works today in the desk-test replay
cons: Passes every tool on the way: 1.1-6.2 s
Selector servo on the spinning rotor needs a slip ring

options.name: Converging cone + funnel cam (tool angles in)
options.principle: Five straight slots tilted 8 deg meet at the barrel's rear mouth. The cartridge slides down its slot, its nose enters the barrel and it straightens as it goes in (nose held by the barrel, tail by the slot). A spring-steel push rod in a PTFE liner, aimed at the chosen slot by a turret, pushes and pulls it.
kill: Size: smallest cone (tilt 8 deg) is 71 mm across and puts the tool tip 299 mm out
Mass 349 g est. against the 350 g cap
options.risk: The tilted cartridge can wedge in the funnel; a push rod in compression can buckle over 194 mm.
pros: Exactly the cam-angled entry described on Nov 21
cons: Neighbouring slots only separate 104 mm from the apex, so the cone is long and wide
Push rod and funnel are the least proven parts

options.name: Fixed ring + turning breech (spin motor selects)
options.principle: Cartridges sit in a fixed ring, spring-fed toward the centre. The barrel runs back as a breech tube with a side window; the spin servo turns the window to the chosen slot, the cartridge drops in and an on-axis rack pushes it out. To put it back, a ramp must drive it sideways into its slot against the spring.
kill: Length: the push rack has to sit behind the breech, so the tool tip is 260 mm out
Return path: no simple way to drive a cartridge sideways out of a turning breech back into its own slot
options.risk: Sideways spring feed and cam-back can jam or put a tool in the wrong slot.
pros: One servo fewer: the spin servo also selects
cons: Putting the tool back into its own slot is the hard, unproven part
Springs push every stored tool against the breech while it spins

options.name: Sliding tray (linear revolver)
options.principle: Five chambers side by side in a flat tray that slides sideways to line one up behind the barrel; a carriage pushes it in as in O1.
kill: Envelope: the tray needs 157 mm of width to slide through (hand base is 41 mm)
options.risk: Sticks out 78 mm each side; snags and hits the other arms.
pros: Flat: could lie along the arm
cons: Heavy guide for the full travel
Ends hit neighbouring arms in a fold
